King County by the numbers

What is King County, Washington, and where does it sit?

King County is the most populous county in Washington, with Seattle as both its seat and its largest city. The 2020 census counted 2,269,675 residents, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 2,344,939.

The Oregon Territory legislature formed the county on December 22, 1852, out of Thurston County, and Seattle became the seat on January 11, 1853. It was first named for William R. King, then vice president-elect, and in 1986 the county government amended the designation to honor Martin Luther King Jr. The county's Wikipedia entry gives a total area of 2,307 square miles, of which 2,116 is land and 191 is water.

The Cascade Range fills the eastern side, and Mount Daniel is the high point at 7,959 feet. The county borders Snohomish, Chelan, Kittitas, Pierce and Kitsap counties, includes Vashon Island and Maury Island in Puget Sound, and has about 760 lakes. Cities inside it include Seattle, Bellevue, Kent, Renton, Redmond, Kirkland, Federal Way, Auburn (partly), Sammamish, Issaquah, Enumclaw, Snoqualmie and North Bend. For a seller, that spread matters because the city and special districts a parcel falls in decide which levies appear on the bill.

Which King County offices handle property tax?

Three separate King County bodies touch your bill: the Department of Assessments sets values, Treasury Operations bills and collects, and the Board of Appeals and Equalization hears valuation disputes. The Board is an independent agency and is not part of the assessor's office.

OfficeWhat it handlesPhone
Department of AssessmentsValues, parcel records, general questions206-296-7300
Assessments, senior exemptionsSenior and disability relief206-296-3920
King County Tax AdvisorAdvice on property tax matters, including appeals206-477-1060
Board of Appeals and EqualizationValuation appeals206-477-3400
Treasury Operations hotlinePayments, statements, account status206-263-2890
Treasury foreclosure unitParcels in or near tax foreclosure206-263-2649

Source: King County 2026 property taxes page and the Treasury FAQ. Treasury is at 201 S. Jackson St., Suite 710, in Seattle's Pioneer Square, and the Customer Service Center on the second floor takes in-person payments on weekdays from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

How much did King County property taxes rise for 2026?

Total property taxes for the 2026 tax year come to $8.4 billion, up about $770 million, or 10%, from $7.7 billion the year before. Countywide taxable value rose about 5.4%, from $873 billion to $920 billion, so the bill grew faster than values.

The Assessor's page attributes most of the increase to voter-approved measures rather than to rising property values. King County itself receives about 20% of the money collected, which pays for services such as roads, criminal justice and public health. The rest goes to the state, cities, schools and other districts.

Measures approved by voters for 2026 include:

  • Seattle: a six-year renewal levy for families, education and preschool, plus a ten-year lid lift for election vouchers.
  • Bothell: a ten-year renewal of the Safe Streets and Sidewalks lid lift.
  • Mercer Island: a $103,160,000 general obligation bond for a new facility.
  • School District 1: replacement capital and education and operations levies.
  • King County: a six-year parks, recreation, trails and open space levy.

Look up your own parcel in the Assessor's eReal Property tool to see its valuation, levy rates and sale history before you set a price.

When are King County property taxes due, and what happens if you miss a date?

The first half is due April 30 and the second half October 31. If a date lands on a weekend or county holiday, payment is due the next business day. King County mails statements once a year, in mid-February, and sends nothing further unless you ask, so sign up for the text or email reminders on the Treasury site.

Miss April 30 and the whole year's tax becomes delinquent on May 1, with late charges worked out monthly on the full-year amount. You can still pay the first half plus charges before October 31. If the second half is missed, monthly charges start November 1 on that unpaid portion. The county says state law bars extensions for hardship or any other reason.

Paying by mail or in person with a check costs nothing extra. Online, the card fee is 2.35% of the charge with a $2 minimum, and an eCheck costs a flat $0.55. A lender that escrows your taxes usually pays in bulk near the deadline, and the county advises contacting the lender if the payment still shows unpaid ten days after the due date.

If you believe a tax is unlawful or excessive and want to keep the right to seek a refund in court, you must hand in a separate written statement at the time you pay, saying you are paying under protest and giving every reason.

How do you appeal a King County property valuation?

Send a petition to the King County Board of Appeals and Equalization after you receive your valuation notice. The board accepts petitions online through eAppeals or by mail with downloadable forms.

The deadline is set by state law in RCW 84.40.038: file by July 1 of the assessment year, or within 30 days of the notice, or within a period of up to 60 days if the county legislative authority has adopted one, whichever is later. Read the date printed on your notice and call the board on 206-477-3400 if it is unclear. The board can waive a late filing for good cause, such as a death or serious illness in the family or a documented postal delay.

A successful appeal is built on market evidence. Useful items include:

  • Recent sales of similar homes in your neighborhood.
  • A contractor's estimate for defects the assessor has not accounted for.
  • An independent appraisal.
  • Photos and records showing a wrong square footage, bedroom count or lot size.

The Assessor also takes petitions for a refund when a manifest error in the property description was used to set value, for example the wrong square footage. The maximum period is six years, depending on the evidence.

What tax relief can a King County homeowner claim?

King County runs a reduction program for owner-occupants who are at least 61, or retired because of a disability, and whose income falls under the state limit. Apply through TaxRelief.kingcounty.gov or call 206-296-3920. The exemption covers one residence and up to one acre, and only the unit the owner lives in qualifies in a multi-family building. Deferral of taxes is available under certain conditions.

Two other programs matter when you sell or renovate. If you add rooms, a deck or a patio to a single-family home, you may apply for a three-year exemption on the value of that improvement, but you must apply before construction is finished. Damaged or destroyed property can qualify for a lower assessed value; the Assessor's office answers questions on 206-263-2332.

What do you owe at closing when you sell a King County house?

The seller usually pays Washington's real estate excise tax, and the amount depends on the sale price. The Department of Revenue says the tax is due to the county treasurer on the date of sale, whenever the deed is recorded, and penalties and interest start if it is not paid within a month. If the seller does not pay, the buyer becomes responsible and the tax can become a lien on the property.

The state portion is graduated. For sales beginning January 1, 2027, the Department of Revenue lists 1.1% up to $551,000, 1.28% from there to $1,551,000, 2.75% to $3,051,000 and 3% above that. A local rate is added on top, so ask the King County Treasury or your closing agent for the combined figure for your city.

Also check the tax statement for non-tax charges that ride on the bill, which vary by location: surface water management, City of Seattle drainage, fire protection, King Conservation District and noxious weed fees. If a new house or addition was never assessed, an omit tax can reach back up to three years and is billed with an extra year to pay.

Can you sell a King County house that is behind on taxes?

Late charges on a delinquent King County parcel keep accruing every month, so ask Treasury for a current figure before you set a closing date. Call the hotline at 206-263-2890, and use 206-263-2649 for any parcel in foreclosure, because foreclosure costs are added and cannot be paid online.

King County offers payment plans for past due prior-year taxes. A plan runs no longer than 12 months, late charges are not reduced, there is a one-time $100 setup fee for each plan, and a vendor adds a monthly processing fee. Taxes three years or more past due can be sent to foreclosure. State law lets an income-qualified owner living in the home ask for interest and penalties to be waived shortly before that three-year mark, as described in RCW 84.56.020.

If the clock is the problem, a direct sale to a cash buyer can close before the tax situation worsens, but compare it with listing on the market and with a payment plan before you decide.

More questions about King County, WA Property Tax Guide

What is the King County property tax deadline in 2026?

The deadlines are April 30 for the first half and October 31 for the second half. October 31, 2026 fell on a Saturday, so the second half was due Monday, November 2 under the county's next-business-day rule. Any second half still unpaid is delinquent, and monthly late charges apply to it.

Where do I file a King County valuation appeal?

File with the King County Board of Appeals and Equalization, online through eAppeals or by mail. It is separate from the Assessor, and its phone number is 206-477-3400.

Who pays real estate excise tax when I sell in King County?

The seller usually pays it, and it is due to the county treasurer on the date of sale. The state rate is graduated by price, and a local rate is added, so get the combined figure from Treasury or your closing agent.

Can seniors lower their King County property tax?

Yes. Owners who live in the home and are at least 61, or retired due to disability, may qualify if income is under the state limit. Apply at TaxRelief.kingcounty.gov or call 206-296-3920.

Does King County offer a payment plan for back taxes?

Yes, for past due prior-year taxes. Plans last up to 12 months, late charges still apply, and there is a one-time $100 setup fee per plan. Call 206-263-2649 or email PaymentPlans@kingcounty.gov.

Skagit County by the numbers

Where is Skagit County and what shapes its property values?

Skagit County is in the Puget Sound region of Washington, and Mount Vernon is both the county seat and its largest city. The Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate counts 132,975 residents across about 1,730 square miles of land.

Four cities (Anacortes, Burlington, Mount Vernon and Sedro-Woolley) and four towns (Concrete, Hamilton, La Conner and Lyman) are incorporated. The county was formed in 1883 from the southern part of Whatcom County. Its land runs from the broad Skagit River valley, a center for tulips, blueberries and strawberries, out to Fidalgo and Guemes islands and east into the Cascade foothills, so a house in Skagit County might sit on a city lot, a farm parcel or an island shoreline.

The Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 figures put the median owner-occupied home at $545,100, and 70.1% of housing units are owner-occupied. Median household income is $89,263. About 25.0% of residents are 65 or older, a share that makes the county's senior exemption (covered below) relevant to a large group of owners.

Which Skagit County offices handle property tax?

Three offices split the work. The Assessor sets values, establishes levies and approves exemptions. The Treasurer sends bills and collects payment. The Board of Equalization is the body that hears value appeals.

OfficeWhat it doesWhere and how to reach it
TreasurerCollects tax, takes payments, answers late-payment questions700 S. 2nd Street, Room 205, Mount Vernon, WA 98273; 360-416-1750; mail to PO Box 518
AssessorValues property, sets levies, approves exemptions360-416-1780; assessor@skagitcountywa.gov
Board of EqualizationHears appeals of assessed value700 S. 2nd Street, Room 100, Mount Vernon; clerk at 360-416-1126

Source: Skagit County Treasurer, Skagit County Assessor FAQ and Board of Equalization guide.

A satellite office in Concrete (45770 A Main Street) also takes payments, in cash, check or money order.

When are Skagit County property taxes due?

Skagit County taxes are due in two installments, April 30 and October 31, and a bill under $50 must be paid in full by April 30 (RCW 84.56.020). The second installment for 2026 was due October 31, 2026, so the next date on the calendar is April 30, 2027.

The county lists these ways to pay:

  • In person at the Treasurer in Mount Vernon with cash, check, money order or card.
  • In a drop box at 700 S. 2nd Street, either at the west end of the horseshoe parking lot or on the second floor outside Room 205 (check or money order only).
  • By phone at 1-866-791-3392, where the processor adds a $3.95 convenience fee plus 2.35% on debit and credit cards or $1.00 on checks.
  • By auto-pay, which withdraws from a U.S. checking or savings account on April 30 and October 31, or the full year on April 30. Enrollment forms are due April 15 for the spring withdrawal and October 15 for the fall one.

Mail carries a trap. The Treasurer warns that the Postal Service no longer guarantees a same-day postmark, and a payment must be postmarked by the due date to count as timely. Mail early, or use a drop box.

What does a late Skagit County tax payment cost?

In Skagit County, interest on a late payment is figured on the full-year tax and starts May 1. Call the Treasurer at 360-416-1750 for the exact payoff figure before you send money.

State law sets the rates. For taxes levied from 2023 on, residential property with four or fewer units and manufactured homes carries 9% annual interest and no penalty. Other real property and personal property carry 12% interest, plus a 3% penalty on tax delinquent on June 1 and another 8% on December 1 (RCW 84.56.020).

A few waivers exist. If the county failed to send the notice, the treasurer must waive interest and penalties. A taxpayer who misses one payment on a personal residence because of a spouse's death, or on a parent's or stepparent's residence after that parent's death, can get interest and penalties waived by telling the treasurer within 60 days of the due date (RCW 84.56.025). The treasurer may also offer payment agreements and accept partial payments, with money applied to the oldest year first.

How do you appeal a Skagit County assessment?

You appeal to the Skagit County Board of Equalization, and the deadline is printed on your Notice of Value. For 2026 values the deadline was Monday, October 26, 2026, so it has passed. That date applied even to owners whose value did not change and who received no notice.

The 2026 notices reflect market value on January 1, 2026 and set the tax payable in 2027. Washington law allows a petition by July 1 or 30 days after the notice was mailed, whichever is later (RCW 84.40.038). The board can waive a late filing if the petition follows within a reasonable time and shows good cause, such as a serious illness or a postal delay documented by the Postal Service. Call the clerk at 360-416-1126 if you think you qualify.

Here is how a hearing works in Skagit County:

  • You get 10 minutes, the Assessor gets 10 minutes, and you then respond.
  • The Assessor's value is presumed correct, and you must show an error with clear, cogent and convincing evidence (RCW 84.40.0301).
  • Strong evidence includes comparable sales near the valuation date, contractor repair estimates and independent appraisals. Listings do not count.
  • Extra documents must arrive 21 business days before the hearing.
  • The county says the whole process can take 6 to 12 months.

Tax amount, personal hardship and the size of the increase are not valid grounds. A losing owner has 30 days to take the case to the Washington State Board of Tax Appeals. The Assessor's next reinspection cycle starts in the Mount Vernon School District and relies on street-level and aerial imagery.

Which relief programs help Skagit County homeowners?

The main program is the Senior and Persons with Disability Property Tax Exemption. The Assessor's page says it covers homeowners age 61 or older, owners with disabilities, and veterans with a 40% VA rating, and that the income limit rises to $78,000 in 2027.

Eligibility uses combined disposable income, which is adjusted gross income plus certain untaxed income such as Social Security, pensions and annuities, counted for everyone who owns and lives in the home. You may subtract a standard deduction of $7,500 per person (you, plus a spouse or domestic partner) or your actual qualifying costs, such as prescriptions, Medicare premiums and care costs. New for 2027, up to $6,000 of rental income from living space in your home can also be subtracted. Call 360-416-1780 to run the worksheet with staff.

Other relief to know about: a tax statement must include a notice about both the exemption and the state deferral program (RCW 84.56.020). If a fire or other event destroys part or all of a property, you can claim a value reduction within three years of the damage (RCW 84.70.010).

What special charges appear on a Skagit County tax bill?

Some line items are special assessments, which sit outside the 1% limit on regular levies. The Assessor does not set them. Each district or program sets its own budget and spreads it by acreage, value or another method.

  • Diking and drainage districts maintain dikes, ditches and pump stations in their area.
  • The Clean Water Assessment funds the county's Clean Water Program, which targets bacterial pollution including Samish Bay shellfish beds, septic repairs and water monitoring.
  • The County Drainage Utility pays for drainage and stormwater work such as pump stations, piping, tide gates and ditches.

Two houses with the same assessed value can pay different totals because each sits in a different mix of city, school, fire and library districts.

How does unpaid tax affect selling a Skagit County house?

Unpaid Skagit County tax has to be cleared from the sale proceeds or the buyer inherits the problem, so ask the Treasurer for a payoff covering every year owed before you accept an offer.

Washington also charges a real estate excise tax on sales, due to the county treasurer on the date of sale whether or not the deed is recorded that day. Usually the seller pays. For sales beginning January 1, 2027, the Department of Revenue lists graduated state rates of 1.1% on the part of the price up to $551,000, 1.28% from $551,000 to $1,551,000, 2.75% from there to $3,051,000 and 3.0% above that. A local rate is added, so ask the Treasurer for the full amount.

Waiting has limits. Once taxes are three years past delinquency, the treasurer must issue certificates of delinquency and begin foreclosure (RCW 84.64.050). An income-qualified owner living in the home may qualify for a waiver of interest and penalties shortly before that three-year mark if foreclosure is under way (RCW 84.56.020).

More questions about Skagit County, WA Property Tax Guide

When are Skagit County property taxes due?

April 30 and October 31, with the full year due April 30 if the bill is under $50. The 2026 second half was due October 31, 2026, so the next due date is April 30, 2027. Late payments carry interest from May 1 on the full-year amount.

Can I still appeal my 2026 Skagit County value?

The published deadline was Monday, October 26, 2026, and it has passed. The Board of Equalization may waive a late filing for good cause, such as serious illness or documented postal delay. Call the clerk at 360-416-1126 to ask, and bring your Notice of Value or parcel number.

What interest rate applies to late Skagit County tax?

For a home with four or fewer units, interest is 9% per year with no penalty. Other property pays 12% per year plus a 3% penalty after June 1 and an additional 8% after December 1. Call the Treasurer at 360-416-1750 for the figure on your parcel.

Who do I call about a Skagit County property tax question?

Call the Treasurer at 360-416-1750 for bills, payments and payoff amounts, and the Assessor at 360-416-1780 for values and exemptions. The Board of Equalization clerk is at 360-416-1126 for appeals.

How long can Skagit County property tax stay unpaid before foreclosure?

The treasurer must start foreclosure by certificate of delinquency once taxes are three years past delinquency, and no certificate may be filed if the delinquent tax is $100 or less (RCW 84.64.050). Sell or pay well before that point, since interest builds every month.

Snohomish County by the numbers

Where is Snohomish County and what drives its housing market?

Snohomish County lies north of Seattle on Puget Sound, with Everett as county seat and largest city. It is the third-most populous county in Washington, at 870,656 people in the Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate, spread over about 2,087 square miles of land. The western side faces Puget Sound and holds most of the people, while the eastern side climbs into the Cascade Range and is largely national forest.

The county has 18 incorporated cities and two towns, Interstate 5 running through it, and the Tulalip Indian Reservation, created by the 1855 Point Elliott Treaty. Boeing began building its Everett assembly plant in 1967, and the Navy opened a homeport in Everett in 1994. Paine Field has had passenger service since March 2019. River valleys such as the Stillaguamish and Snohomish are farmed and occasionally flood during major weather events like atmospheric rivers.

Census figures for 2020 to 2024 give a median owner-occupied home value of $696,000, a median household income of $111,246 and an owner-occupied rate of 68.2%. The mean commute is 30.8 minutes.

Which Snohomish County offices handle property tax?

The Assessor sets the value of taxable property, taxing district budgets and voter-approved measures determine the levy, and the Treasurer calculates and sends the bill. A separate Board of Equalization hears value appeals.

  • Assessor: main line 425-388-3433, residential appraisal 425-388-6555, commercial 425-388-3390, exemptions 425-388-3540.

When are Snohomish County property taxes due?

First-half or full-year Snohomish County tax is due April 30, and the second half is due October 31. Taxes under $50 for the year are due in full by April 30. The October 31, 2026 date has passed, so the next deadline is April 30, 2027.

By mail, a payment must be postmarked on or before the due date or the tax becomes delinquent. Online payments must be completed by the due date too. The Treasurer advises mailing several days early because of a change in the Postal Service postmark process, or asking a post office for a hand-stamped postmark or using certified mail. Allow 7 to 10 business days for a mailed payment to clear. A tax payment drop box on the county campus is open around the clock for checks; keep payments out of the ballot drop box.

The Treasurer's office has been moving to new software through summer 2026, and its page warns of delays on some requests, with electronic statements and account log-in unavailable at that time. If you need a payoff figure for a sale, call 425-388-3366 early.

What does late payment cost in Snohomish County?

If the first half is not paid by April 30, the full year's tax becomes delinquent, and interest or penalty is figured on the whole amount. Snohomish County assesses delinquent charges on the first day of each month.

The rate depends on the type of property. Under RCW 84.56.020, a home with four or fewer units, including a manufactured home, pays 9% annual interest and no penalty on taxes levied in 2023 or later. Other real property and personal property pay 12% interest, with a 3% penalty after June 1 and another 8% after December 1.

State law lets the treasurer waive interest and penalties when the county's own error kept a notice from reaching you, or when a spouse's death, or a parent's or stepparent's death, caused a missed payment on a personal residence and you notify the treasurer within 60 days (RCW 84.56.025). Payment agreements and partial payments are also allowed, with money going to the oldest year first.

How does the Snohomish County Assessor set a home's value?

The Assessor must value property at 100% of true and fair market value as of January 1. Snohomish County moved to annual revaluation with the 2004 assessment, so every property is appraised each year rather than in a four-year cycle. That means a falling market can lower values the next year and a rising one raises them.

Your tax is a share of what the taxing districts levy. The Assessor's value decides your share, while district budgets and voter-approved levies decide the total. Regular levies are limited to a 1% annual increase without a public vote. A value increase therefore does not always mean a tax increase of the same size.

Because assessments follow the calendar, sales in one year set the January 1 value of the next year and the taxes due the year after. This lag is built into the system and applies whether the market is rising or falling.

How do you appeal a Snohomish County assessment?

File a petition with the Board of Equalization within 60 calendar days of the date on your Notice of Value, or by July 1 of the assessment year if no notice was sent, whichever is later. State law lets a county adopt a limit of up to 60 days, and Snohomish County has. There is no filing fee, and you submit a separate petition for each parcel.

The county's appeal guide lays out the steps:

  • Petition forms can be filed electronically on the county website until 4:00 PM on the deadline day, or on paper by mail or in person.
  • You receive a case number, and the Assessor reviews your petition. If you and the Assessor agree on a value, you sign a stipulation and the case closes.
  • If not, you get a hearing date about 60 days ahead. Hearings are held on Zoom, with in-person attendance possible if you tell the clerk at least a week before.
  • Evidence goes to both the board and the Assessor at least 21 business days before the hearing, up to 75 pages, with no audio, video or web links.
  • Decisions arrive by mail within 45 calendar days of the hearing.

The assessed value is presumed correct, so you carry the burden of clear, cogent and convincing evidence (RCW 84.40.0301). The board cannot use list prices, your ability to pay or the size of the increase. The best evidence is comparable sales near January 1, errors in square footage or other property records, and contractor bids for major repairs. Either side may appeal the board's decision to the State Board of Tax Appeals within 30 days of the mailing date. A decision affects only the assessment year appealed.

Which tax relief programs apply in Snohomish County?

The Assessor runs a senior citizen and disabled person exemption, and the county page for 2024 lists a maximum disposable income of $75,000. Call 425-388-3540 or email assessor@snoco.org to learn the current limit, and use the county's status tool to follow an application.

Exempt participants are taxed on the lower of the frozen value from the date they qualified or the new market value. A state deferral program also exists for eligible seniors and disabled owners, and the tax statement must carry a notice describing both programs (RCW 84.56.020). Deferred tax becomes a lien on the property, and it must be repaid at transfer of ownership, which matters to any seller who deferred.

Open space and historic property programs carry their own dates. The county calendar sets October 1 as the last day to file for an exemption on historic property and December 31 as the open space application deadline.

What happens to Snohomish County tax when you sell?

Any tax still owed on a Snohomish County house must be paid out of the sale, so get a payoff for every unpaid year from the Treasurer before the closing date. Delinquent interest accrues from the first of each month, which makes a quote good only for the month it is issued.

The Department of Revenue says real estate excise tax is due to the county treasurer on the date of sale, and the seller usually pays. The state portion is graduated, and for sales from January 1, 2027 it starts at 1.1% on the first $551,000 and climbs in steps to 3.0% on any amount over $3,051,000. The local rate is added. Ask the Treasurer for the combined figure.

If delinquent tax sits for three years, RCW 84.64.050 requires the treasurer to issue certificates of delinquency and start foreclosure. A county cannot file a certificate when the delinquent tax is $100 or less. An income-qualified owner living in the home can have interest and penalties waived once foreclosure is under way (RCW 84.56.020).

More questions about Snohomish County, WA Property Tax Guide

When are Snohomish County property taxes due?

April 30 for the first half or the full year, and October 31 for the second half. Taxes under $50 are due in full by April 30. The October 31, 2026 date has passed, and the next is April 30, 2027.

How long do I have to appeal a Snohomish County property value?

You have 60 calendar days from the date on your Notice of Value, or until July 1 of the assessment year, whichever is later. File with the Board of Equalization at 425-388-3407. There is no fee, and each parcel needs its own petition.

What is the interest on late Snohomish County property tax?

For a home with four or fewer units, interest is 9% a year with no penalty. Other property pays 12% a year, plus a 3% penalty after June 1 and 8% after December 1. If the first half is not paid by April 30, the full year becomes delinquent.

Can I sell a Snohomish County house with back taxes?

Yes, as long as the unpaid tax, interest and penalties are paid from the proceeds at closing. Call the Treasurer at 425-388-3366 for a payoff for every year owed. Start early, since the office has warned about delays tied to a software change in summer 2026.

Where do I pay Snohomish County property tax?

Pay online through the Treasurer's payment site, by card over the phone at 833-440-3332, by mail, or in the campus drop box in Everett. Mail should be sent several days early, and mailed payments can take 7 to 10 business days to clear.

Franklin County by the numbers

What is Franklin County, Washington, and who lives there?

Franklin County is a south-central Washington county whose seat and largest city is Pasco. It is one corner of the Tri-Cities, alongside Kennewick and Richland in neighboring Benton County, and the 2020 census counted 96,749 residents, up from 78,163 in 2010.

The county was formed out of Whitman County on November 28, 1883, and named it for Benjamin Franklin. The county's Wikipedia entry gives a total area of about 1,265 square miles, nearly all of it land. Neighbors are Adams County to the north, Whitman to the east, Walla Walla and Columbia to the southeast, Benton to the southwest and Grant to the northwest.

Franklin County has four incorporated cities: Pasco, Connell, Mesa and Kahlotus. Basin City and West Pasco are census-designated places, and Eltopia, Farrington and Harder are unincorporated communities. State Route 260, Interstate 182, U.S. 12 and U.S. 395 are the major highways.

In 2020 the county had 29,740 housing units, 3.3% of them vacant, and 68.3% of occupied homes were owner-occupied. About 88.6% of residents lived in urban areas.

Which Franklin County offices handle property tax?

The Assessor values property, the Board of Equalization hears appeals, and the Treasurer bills and collects. The Assessor and the Board of Equalization sit in the Franklin County Courthouse at 1016 N 4th Avenue in Pasco.

  • Assessor: Room A-104 in the basement. Phone 509-545-3506, weekdays 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. The county assessor is John A. Rosenau.
  • Board of Equalization: Room A102. Phone 509-546-5855 weekdays 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m., or email boeclerk@franklincountywa.gov.
  • Treasurer: collects both tax installments and runs the county's tax sales. Online account tools, a drive-up drop box and a paperless billing portal are available.

The Assessor's office does not set the amount of tax or send bills. Taxpayers, state limits and each taxing district's assessed value decide the rate, and the Treasurer bills and collects it.

How often does Franklin County revalue a house?

Every parcel is inspected in person at least once every six years, and values are updated countywide each year through statistical analysis of sales. If similar properties in an area keep selling above or below their assessed values, the roll for that area is adjusted. Remodels, additions and subdivisions get a fresh value.

Under RCW 84.40.020, real property is valued as of January 1 for taxes payable the following year. The Assessor mails Real Property Change of Value Notices in the third quarter, and the Treasurer mails tax statements in February. The notice you receive in summer reflects the prior year's market data, so a quick market change may not show up yet.

The Assessor uses three methods: sales comparison and cost for most homes, and the income approach mainly for business property. Before you list, compare the square footage, bedroom count and heating type on the record with the real house, since a wrong detail can raise or lower the number.

When are Franklin County property taxes due, and what do late payments cost?

How do you appeal a Franklin County assessment?

Begin with the Assessor. Call 509-545-3506 or visit Room A-104, review the appraisal, and ask the appraiser to compare sale prices of similar properties or visit the house. If that does not settle it, file a taxpayer petition with the Franklin County Board of Equalization.

The petition must be mailed within 30 days of the change of value notice or by July 1 of the assessment year, whichever is later. When the last day lands on a weekend or holiday, the deadline moves to the next business day, and a mailed petition must carry a postmark no later than the deadline. Each parcel takes its own form.

Evidence such as appraisals, maps, pictures and letters is due 21 days before the hearing. The Board presumes the Assessor's value is correct, and under WAC 458-14-046 you must show clear, cogent and convincing evidence that it is wrong. Filing a protective appeal within the deadline keeps your rights alive for the year, even if you are still gathering proof. In recent cycles, board sessions have run from October into January.

What tax relief does Franklin County offer?

The Assessor lists several state programs, and each starts with a call to 509-545-3506.

  • Exemptions for senior citizens and disabled persons.
  • Exemptions for qualifying nonprofit property.
  • A destroyed property claim, which adjusts the value of damaged buildings.
  • A historical restoration exemption for significant property under restoration.
  • Open space classification for agricultural land, timberland and nature preserves.

Nonprofit exemption applications must reach the Department of Revenue by March 31, and farm open space applications are deemed approved on May 1 unless the Assessor notifies you otherwise.

How do you pay Franklin County taxes?

Since January 1, 2024, the Treasurer's Office no longer takes payments by phone. Use the online portal, mail a check or pay in person. There is a drive-up drop box under the blue banner across from the security building.

You can register for email reminders each April and October through the paperless tax bill page, and the office will help you set up the account. It also offers a variety of payment plan options, so call before an account falls far behind. Address changes go through the Assessor's page, after you confirm the address with the postal service.

When a parcel goes to a tax sale, the county advertises it at least three weeks ahead in the Franklin County Graphic and the Tri-City Herald. State law lets the treasurer foreclose on parcels with unpaid taxes, so an old balance deserves attention.

What do you owe when you sell a Franklin County house?

Washington charges a real estate excise tax on the sale, and the seller usually pays. The tax is due to the treasurer of the county where the property sits on the date of sale, regardless of when the deed is recorded, and a month's delay brings interest and penalties.

The Department of Revenue sets the state portion on a sliding scale by price, with breakpoints at $551,000, $1,551,000 and $3,051,000 for sales beginning January 1, 2027. A local rate is added to that. Ask the Franklin County Treasurer or your closing agent for the combined rate for Pasco or the other town where the home sits, and for a payoff figure on any tax still owed.

Grant County by the numbers

Where is Grant County, Washington, and how did it form?

Grant County sits in central Washington, with Ephrata as the county seat and Moses Lake as the largest city. The state legislature created it on February 24, 1909, carving it out of Douglas County, and named it for Ulysses S. Grant.

According to the county's Wikipedia entry, Grant County covers 2,791 square miles, of which 2,680 is land, making it the fourth-largest county in the state by area. Its neighbors are Douglas County to the north, Okanogan to the northeast, Lincoln and Adams to the east, Franklin to the southeast, Benton to the south, Yakima to the southwest and Kittitas to the west.

Incorporated places include Electric City, Ephrata, George, Grand Coulee, Mattawa, Moses Lake, Quincy, Royal City, Soap Lake and Warden, plus the towns of Coulee City, Coulee Dam (partly), Hartline, Krupp and Wilson Creek. Landmarks that shape where people live include the Columbia River, Moses Lake, Potholes Reservoir, Soap Lake and the Grand Coulee. The Cascades block most coastal rain, which gives the county hot summers and cold winters.

What shapes the Grant County economy and housing stock?

Farming and irrigation drive much of it. Wikipedia reports that Grant County is the top crop-producing county in the state and a large source of Washington's hay, and a sign on I-90 at the county line calls it the nation's leading potato-producing county.

The reason is water. Dryland farming gave way to irrigation after the first large-scale attempts in 1898, and the Columbia Basin Project, built around Grand Coulee Dam, changed the region for good after its approval in 1933. Towns such as Quincy, Ephrata and Wilson Creek grew alongside the railroads that carried crops out.

The 2020 census counted 99,123 residents and 38,635 housing units. About 62.2% of occupied homes were owner-occupied, and 11.8% of all units were vacant. School districts serving the county include Moses Lake, Ephrata, Quincy, Othello, Wahluke, Royal, Soap Lake, Warden, Grand Coulee Dam, Coulee-Hartline, Almira, Odessa and Wilson Creek. Which district a house sits in changes the levies on its tax bill, so check the parcel record before you price it.

Which Grant County offices deal with property tax?

The Assessor values property and the Treasurer bills and collects the tax. The Assessor tracks about 61,570 parcels, keeps ownership and legal descriptions up to date, and does not set the tax amount. Voters, state limits and the assessed value in each district set the rate.

  • Assessor: Courthouse Annex, Room 107, 35 C Street NW, Ephrata. Phone 509-754-2013, weekdays 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. The current assessor is Melissa McKnight.
  • Treasurer: 35 C Street NW, Room 204, Ephrata, mailing address P.O. Box 37. Phone 509-754-2010, weekdays 8 a.m. to noon and 1 to 5 p.m.
  • Board of Equalization: hears valuation appeals. The Assessor's Office, at 509-754-2011 ext. 2683, helps owners find comparable sales.

The Treasurer's page links to a searchable tax statement for 2025 and 2026, and a parcel lookup, so you can pull a payoff picture without visiting. Mailing address changes and the quit claim forms mentioned below also go through that office.

How does the Grant County Assessor value a house?

Real property is valued as of January 1, and the Assessor revalues properties every year. The county's FAQ says you need to file a new petition each year to protect your appeal rights, because a prior-year appeal does not carry over.

Two programs have dates worth knowing if you own an older home or farmland. Senior and disabled tax deferral applications are due April 1 under state law, while claims for the senior and disabled exemption are accepted all year for taxes payable the following year. Open space (current use) applications are deemed approved on May 1 unless the Assessor says otherwise, and the window to apply for the next year's valuation runs from January 1 through December 31.

The Assessor's page lists a senior exemption press release for the 2027 tax year. Ask the office for the current income limit before you rely on any figure.

What are the key Grant County property tax dates?

First-half tax is due April 30 and second-half tax is due October 31, and the Treasurer accepts a postmark from the post office. Late payments pick up interest, and some property types pick up penalties as well.

Source: Grant County Assessor's important dates and RCW 84.56.020. The penalties do not apply to residential property of four or fewer units, which pays interest only, set at 9% a year for taxes levied in 2023 and later. Other property pays 12% a year plus the two penalties.

How do you appeal a Grant County assessment?

Start by calling the Assessor, then file a petition with the Grant County Board of Equalization. It must arrive by July 1 of the assessment year or within 30 calendar days after the date of the value change notice, whichever is later, and a mailed petition must be postmarked by then. Filing is free, and each parcel needs its own petition.

  • Include the parcel number, your name and address, a property description, the Assessor's value, your opinion of value and your reasons, signed and dated, with a copy of the notice.
  • Add comparable sales, repair estimates, an appraisal or photos. The Board weighs sales closest to January 1.
  • Submit extra evidence at least 21 business days before the hearing.

The assessor's value is presumed correct, and you carry the burden of showing otherwise with clear, cogent and convincing evidence. Hardship and the size of the tax bill cannot be considered. You get at least 30 business days' notice of the hearing, and decisions usually arrive within about two weeks, though the statute allows 45 days. Either side can appeal to the state Board of Tax Appeals within 30 days of the decision.

How do you pay Grant County taxes, and what if you are behind?

Pay by mail, in person or through Point & Pay. Online fees are 2.7% for credit cards, 0.95% for debit and $1.30 for an eCheck, and a returned payment carries a $30 fee. Payments can take three to five business days to show.

The Treasurer posts a delinquent tax payment plan application and an interest waiver application for a principal residence heading into foreclosure. The office also runs an annual tax foreclosure sale: the 2026 sale was held November 9 and 10 on the Public Surplus website, so it has already taken place. If your tax is far behind, call the Treasurer on 509-754-2010 well before any sale date, since state law allows an income-qualified owner living in the home to seek a waiver of interest and penalties shortly before the third anniversary of delinquency.

What happens at closing when you sell a Grant County house?

The deed and a real estate excise tax affidavit go to the Treasurer in the county where the property sits. The Treasurer's page links the state forms, the exemption code list and a lack of probate affidavit used with a deed when no probate was opened.

The Department of Revenue says the seller usually pays this tax and it is due on the date of sale. State thresholds are graduated by price, and a local rate is added, so ask the Treasurer for the combined rate that applies to your city. Blank deed and quit claim forms are listed there too, and a title company or attorney can draft a deed if yours needs one.

Half is due April 30 and the other half October 31. The Treasurer accepts a postmark from the post office, and any amount still unpaid after the dates carries interest.

How long do I have to appeal my Grant County assessment?

Until July 1 of the assessment year or 30 calendar days after the value change notice, whichever is later. Mailed petitions must be postmarked by that date, and filing costs nothing.

Does Grant County revalue homes every year?

Yes. The Assessor revalues properties each year, and you must file a fresh petition each year to protect your appeal rights.

How much does it cost to pay Grant County taxes online?

Credit cards carry 2.7%, debit cards 0.95% and eChecks $1.30. Checks by mail or in person carry no vendor fee.

Yes. The Treasurer held it on November 9 and 10 on the Public Surplus website, so it has passed. Contact the Treasurer at 509-754-2010 about the next one.

Spokane County by the numbers

Where is Spokane County and who lives there?

Spokane County is in eastern Washington, with the city of Spokane as both county seat and largest city. The Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 558,344 residents, which makes it the fourth-most populous county in the state, and it covers about 1,764 square miles of land. Mount Spokane, at 5,883 feet, is the highest point.

The county was created by the territorial legislature in 1858 from part of Walla Walla County, was attached to Stevens County for a time, and became separate again on October 30, 1879. Outside the city, residential communities include Nine Mile Falls, Newman Lake, Greenacres, Peone and Veradale. Schools are divided among many districts, among them Spokane Public Schools, Central Valley, Mead, East Valley, West Valley, Cheney, Deer Park and Medical Lake, and the district you live in affects the school levy on your bill.

Census figures for 2020 to 2024 show a median owner-occupied home value of $410,700, a median household income of $78,582 and an owner-occupied rate of 64.5%. The county had 241,434 housing units in 2025, and the Assessor says it appraises about 212,000 real property parcels.

Which Spokane County offices handle property tax?

The Assessor values property, the Treasurer bills and collects, and the Board of Equalization is an independent body that handles appeals. About 56 taxing districts in the county send budgets to the Assessor each November, and the Assessor turns them into levy rates in January.

  • Treasurer: Spokane County Courthouse, 1116 W. Broadway Ave., Spokane, WA 99260; 509-477-4713; treasurer@spokanecounty.gov; open Monday through Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.
  • Assessor: 509-477-3698 for ownership, values and exemptions; 509-477-4787 for business personal property.
  • Mail payments go to the Spokane County Treasurer, P.O. Box 199, Spokane, WA 99210.

The Treasurer's office will be closed Thursday and Friday, November 26 and 27, 2026, for Thanksgiving, and reopens Monday, November 30, at 8:30 a.m.

When are Spokane County property taxes due?

Spokane County taxes are due in two halves, April 30 and October 31. If the total is under $50, the whole amount is due April 30. A due date that lands on a weekend or county holiday moves to the next business day. October 31, 2026 fell on a Saturday, and the second half for 2026 is now past.

The county mails one statement a year with a coupon for each half. If you have not received it by March 31, call 509-477-4713 or look it up on the SCOUT site, because a missing statement does not excuse late payment. Owners who pay through a mortgage escrow still receive a full statement, and under Washington law it is the taxpayer's responsibility to make sure the tax is paid.

Payment options include online (eCheck, debit or credit card), phone, mail, the courthouse, and two drop boxes at the courthouse that take checks only. In April and October the Treasurer also collects in person at Spokane Valley City Hall and the North Spokane Library on set dates. Online fees are charged by the vendor: 45 cents per eCheck transaction, and 2.65% on cards with a $1.00 minimum. Mailed payments are sorted by federal postmark under RCW 1.12.070, and a postage meter date does not count, so mail early.

What happens when a Spokane County payment is late?

First-half tax becomes delinquent on May 1 and second-half tax on November 1. Interest is figured on the full year's tax.

PenaltyNone3% on June 1 and 8% on December 1

Source: Spokane County Treasurer, Homeowner Information. Taxes billed before 2023 accrue at 1% per month.

The county says it cannot waive interest or penalty when it mailed the statement to an address supplied by the taxpayer or a taxpayer's agent, such as a closing agent. A hardship waiver exists for a personal residence if the death of a spouse, parent or stepparent caused the missed payment, but the treasurer must be told within 60 days of the due date and the tax paid within that time (RCW 84.56.025). To keep a right to sue for a refund, a payment under protest must be put in writing and included with the payment (RCW 84.68.020). A returned bank item adds a $30 fee.

How does the Spokane County Assessor value a house?

The Assessor values every real property parcel each year as of January 1, and physically inspects each at least once every six years. New construction is appraised annually, and owners are notified when a value changes. State law requires 100% of true and fair market value, based on comparable sales, depreciated replacement cost or income methods.

The Official Assessment Notice arrives in June, but levy rates are not calculated until mid-January of the following year, so the notice cannot tell you the final tax. Individual bills are not capped at a 1% increase. That limit applies to some taxing district budgets, and special levies, banked capacity and annexations complicate it.

When a market cools or stalls, assessed values follow. The Assessor's office says its values reflect sales information, and a flat local market produces flat assessments.

How do you appeal a Spokane County assessment?

You appeal to the County Board of Equalization by July 1 of the assessment year or within 30 days of the date the Change of Value Notice was mailed, whichever is later. A mailed petition must be postmarked by midnight of the deadline, or you can hand-deliver it and have it date-stamped. The filing is free, and a letter or phone call does not replace the petition form.

  • Your petition must give specific reasons the value is wrong, with the parcel number, the Assessor's value and your own estimate. Tax amount, other properties' values, the size of the increase and hardship cannot be considered.
  • Extra evidence must reach the board at least seven business days before the hearing.
  • You are notified of the hearing 15 business days ahead, and a written decision usually follows within about two weeks.
  • You may settle with the Assessor by a stipulation of value, or end the appeal by withdrawal.
  • You have 30 calendar days to appeal the board's decision to the State Board of Tax Appeals, or you can pay under protest and sue for a refund under chapter 84.68 RCW.

The assessor is presumed correct, and you need clear, cogent and convincing evidence (RCW 84.40.0301). Keep paying while the case is open. One exception matters to buyers: the board can reconvene after the deadline if a new purchaser bought after July 1 and before December 31 of the assessment year at less than 90% of the assessed value.

Which relief programs help Spokane County homeowners?

The Assessor's FAQ describes a senior exemption for owner-occupants age 62 or older with household income under $50,000, available through an application on the Assessor's forms page or by calling 509-477-3698. The Treasurer's site adds that Senate Bill 6162, signed after the 2026 session, sets new income thresholds for the senior and disabled persons exemption starting in 2027. Call the Assessor for the current limits, since the numbers are changing.

The exemption also reaches people retired due to disability and certain veterans. A processed application produces a corrected statement from the Treasurer for you or your mortgage company. State law additionally requires every tax statement to describe the exemption and the deferral program (RCW 84.56.020).

If you pay off a mortgage during the year, you must contact the Treasurer to update billing information and request a duplicate bill. Failure to receive a bill does not cancel interest and penalty charges.

What should you know about back taxes before selling in Spokane County?

Get a written payoff for every unpaid year from the Treasurer before closing, and have the closing agent pay it from the proceeds. Because interest accrues monthly, the figure changes each month.

The county's own rule about mailed statements has a closing-day consequence: if the Treasurer mails a bill to the address a closing agent provided and it goes unpaid, the county cannot waive the interest. Make sure your agent has the right parcel number and a forwarding address that works.

Real estate excise tax is due to the county treasurer on the date of sale, usually from the seller. The state portion is graduated. In the schedule for sales from January 1, 2027, the 1.28% bracket applies to the price between $551,000 and $1,551,000, and the local rate comes on top. Ask the Treasurer for the total.

If taxes stay unpaid for three years from delinquency, RCW 84.64.050 requires the treasurer to issue certificates of delinquency and begin foreclosure. Payments on past-due taxes must include the oldest delinquent year, with interest and penalties, before a certificate is filed or property is distrained (RCW 84.56.020).

More questions about Spokane County, WA Property Tax Guide

When are Spokane County property taxes due?

April 30 for the first half and October 31 for the second half. A bill under $50 is due in full April 30. The October 31, 2026 date has passed, and the next is April 30, 2027, or the next business day if that date falls on a weekend.

What if I never received my Spokane County tax statement?

Call the Treasurer at 509-477-4713 or find the statement on the SCOUT site if it has not arrived by March 31. A missing bill does not cancel interest or penalty, because it remains your responsibility to see the tax is paid.

How long do I have to appeal my Spokane County assessment?

Until July 1 of the assessment year or 30 days after the Change of Value Notice was mailed, whichever is later. File the Board of Equalization petition form, which is free, and keep paying your tax while the appeal runs.

What interest does Spokane County charge on late tax?

A home with four or fewer units pays 0.75% a month with no penalty. Other property pays 1% a month plus a 3% penalty on June 1 and 8% on December 1. Interest is calculated on the full year's tax, starting May 1 for the first half.

Can I sell a Spokane County house that owes back taxes?

Yes, if the unpaid tax, interest and penalties are paid at closing. Get a payoff from the Treasurer at 509-477-4713, and note that three years of delinquency lets the county begin foreclosure. Pay or sell before then.

Douglas County by the numbers

Where is Douglas County, Washington, and what towns does it include?

Douglas County lies on the Columbia River in north-central Washington. Waterville is the county seat, but East Wenatchee is the largest settlement, and the county is part of the Wenatchee metropolitan statistical area.

The county was created out of Lincoln County on November 28, 1883, and named for the statesman Stephen A. Douglas. The county's Wikipedia entry lists a total area of 1,849 square miles, of which 1,819 is land. Okanogan County lies to the north, Grant to the south, Kittitas to the southwest and Chelan to the west. U.S. 2 and U.S. 97 are the main highways.

Three cities sit inside the county: Bridgeport, East Wenatchee and Rock Island. Mansfield, Waterville and part of Coulee Dam are towns. Unincorporated communities include Beebe, Douglas, Lamoine, Leahy, Orondo, Palisades and Withrow. The city or town a parcel falls in matters when you sell, because the local excise tax rate changes by location.

How many people live in Douglas County, and how many own their homes?

The 2020 census counted 42,938 residents in Douglas County, up from 38,431 in 2010, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 46,473. About 74.6% of residents lived in urban areas and 25.4% in rural ones.

The county had 17,318 housing units in 2020, of which 11.0% were vacant. Among occupied units, 70.7% were owner-occupied and 29.3% were rented. About 18.0% of residents were 65 or older.

Which Douglas County offices handle property tax?

Douglas County splits the work among the Assessor, the Treasurer, the Auditor and a Board of Equalization. Most offices sit in Waterville on South Rainier Street.

  • Assessor: 213 S Rainier Street, mailing address P.O. Box 387, Waterville. Phone 509-745-8521, weekdays 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The assessor is Jim Ruud.
  • Treasurer: same building, mailing address P.O. Box 609. Phone 509-745-8525. Felisha L. Rosales is the treasurer. The office also collects excise tax for the state and runs tax foreclosures.
  • Auditor: records deeds. Phone 509-745-8527.
  • Board of Equalization: 203 S Rainier, Waterville, P.O. Box 747. Phone 509-745-8537.

The Treasurer also works under contract for five irrigation districts in the county, so some bills carry irrigation charges alongside the property tax.

How does the Douglas County Assessor value a house?

Washington requires the Assessor to value property at 100% of market value, and Douglas County revalues every property each year. The Assessor's page invites owners to call 509-745-8521 to discuss a valuation before appealing.

Tax breaks start with age and income. Residents 61 or older, people retired because of a disability, and veterans with a qualifying disability may be eligible for a senior property tax exemption depending on household income. The Assessor's page links an online screening tool, but the office makes the final call. Agricultural land may qualify for open space treatment, and the Assessor has forms for current use, parcel combinations, destroyed property and address changes.

Property tax pays for cities, the county, fire protection, law enforcement, libraries, parks, roads and schools. Which of those a parcel pays for depends on where it sits.

When are Douglas County property taxes due, and how can you pay?

The first half was due April 30, 2026, and the second half October 31, 2026. October 31 fell on a Saturday this year, so ask the Treasurer how a payment dated Monday, November 2 is handled if you have not yet paid.

The Treasurer takes payment through Point and Pay by phone at 866-898-2916 or online through the TaxSifter parcel search. Payments must be processed before 11:59 p.m. Pacific time to count as same day, but they are not posted in real time, so allow two to three business days. Vendor fees are a flat $2.30 for an eCheck, 2.7% for a credit card and 0.95% for a debit card. A live-agent Personal Teller service costs an extra $5.

Under RCW 84.56.020, a missed first half makes the whole year's tax delinquent, and interest is computed monthly. Residential property of four units or fewer pays 9% a year and no penalties, while other property pays 12% plus penalties of 3% and then 8%.

How do you appeal a Douglas County assessment?

Douglas County's Board of Equalization is made up of the county commissioners. The county hires an independent hearing examiner to run the hearings and recommend a decision, and the board and clerk operate separately from the Assessor.

File a complete petition by July 1 of the assessment year, or within 30 days of the mailing date printed on your Change of Value Notice, whichever is later. The petition must be filed or postmarked by then.

  • Email: BOE@CO.DOUGLAS.WA.US, received by 5 p.m.
  • Mail: Douglas County Board of Equalization, P.O. Box 747, Waterville, WA 98858.
  • Walk-in only: Public Service Building, 140 19th Street NW, East Wenatchee.

Pay your taxes on time even while an appeal is pending. If the value drops, the county credits your account for the difference. A late filing can sometimes be excused for good cause, and Douglas County provides a waiver of late filing request form for that purpose.

What excise tax applies when you sell a Douglas County house?

Washington's real estate excise tax applies to every sale unless an exemption fits, and the tax is the seller's responsibility under WAC 458-61A-301. The Douglas County Treasurer collects it as the state's agent, and the sale must be presented within 30 days of the sale date to avoid interest and penalties.

You bring the excise tax affidavit and the deed to the Treasurer first, then to the Auditor for recording. Plan time for it: processing takes 10 to 20 minutes per document, service is first come first served, and the Auditor stops recording at 4 p.m. Title companies and attorneys can file electronically through Simplifile. Courthouse staff cannot draft or review a deed, and mobile or manufactured home sales have special requirements, so call 509-745-8525.

What happens if a Douglas County house is behind on taxes?

The Treasurer has the legal duty to foreclose, seize and sell property for delinquent taxes. Before that point, state law lets the Treasurer accept payment agreements and partial payments, applied to the oldest year first. Call 509-745-8525 for a payoff figure before you set a closing date. Interest is computed monthly, so the figure changes from one month to the next.

Credit cards carry a 2.7% vendor fee and debit cards 0.95%. An eCheck is a flat $2.30.
